Arizona Republicans Use School Children In "Anti-Drug" Rally
Against "Medical Marijuana" – Or Something

(Ed. note: A child is a small human being to be used as a prop or other device in prohibitionist propaganda. When you lie to several of them at one time and get them to respond in public, it is called an "anti-drug rally." When you lie to them in private and expect them to keep quiet, it is called "drug education."  When the prohibitionist propaganda is paid for with government money it is called "demand reduction." When you arrest them or their parents, it is called "for their own good." When you make them take dangerous pharmaceuticals in stead of medical marijuana, it is called "science.")

PROPOSITION 300 PROMPTS ANTI-DRUG RALLY
See

Republican leaders rallied in front of 150 children at the Thomas J. Pappas school for the homeless Monday, urging a "yes" vote on Proposition 300, to gut Arizona’s medical-marijuana law.
(Ed. note: If it is defeated, it will be called a rejection of "medical marijuana" but the bill does far more than make marijuana medically available, and it does that under restrictions that make it unworkable.)
See
Arizona Paper Carries Column by Rhode Island Editor Endorsing Prop 200 – Without Mentioning Medical Marijuana

Proclaiming that drugs are bad and cheerleading the children

Supporters of the 1996 medical-marijuana initiative want to legalize street drugs and to use the legalization of those drugs as medicine as an opening wedge, the children were told.

University of Phoenix founder John Sperling and millionaires from New York and Cleveland have spent more than $1 million for the initiative and against a Nov. 3 referendum on changes made by the Legislature, said Stan Barnes, president of Arizonans Against Heroin and an announcer on KFYI-AM (910).

(Ed. note: When you don’t tell your readers about the use of government funding for prohibitionist propaganda it is called "journalism.")

Proposition 300 would require Food and Drug Administration approval of marijuana as medicine before Arizona doctors could prescribe street drugs for side effects of cancer, AIDS and other ailments.
(Ed. note: "Street drugs??" The proper term is Schedule I drugs. Street drugs is the prohibitionist term for them intended to influence the public against them.)

If Proposition 300 fails, the 1996 law would remain in effect.

Sam Vagenas, consultant to The People Have Spoken, said using the tax-supported school for the rally was an "abuse of public power."

"If there’s no law against it, there ought to be," said Vagenas, whose group opposes Proposition 300. "If we called up to do a press conference at the school, they wouldn’t let us do it, and we certainly wouldn’t do it."

Maricopa County schools Superintendent Sandra Dowling said she would allow Vagenas’ group to present an anti-drug message to students.
